summary: A poem of wrath, grief, honor, and shame, in which Achilles' anger and his love for Patroclus drive slaughter, fear, and finally pity.

need-to-breathe.why: Achilles nearly drowns when the river Scamander rises against him, and dying warriors gasp out their lives, but breath itself is seldom at issue.

hungry.why: Odysseus insists the army eat before battle while the grieving Achilles refuses all food, and Priam and Achilles share a meal before Hector's body is returned.

full.why: The formula that the heroes feast until they have put away desire for eating and drinking recurs at every meal, but satiety carries no weight.

thirsty.why: No character is deprived of water; the Scamander is a battlefield and a god, never a source of thirst.

gassy.why: Nothing in the poem concerns intestinal gas.

need-to-poop.why: No character needs to defecate; the ox dung Ajax falls into at the games belongs to disgust, not to this feel.

sleepy.why: Hera enlists Sleep to put Zeus under, Rhesus and the Thracians are slaughtered in their sleep, and Achilles lies sleepless with grief for Patroclus.

nauseous.why: No character sickens from food or poison; the plague of Book 1 kills rather than nauseates, and Hector vomiting blood is injury, not nausea.

urge-to-sneeze.why: No sneeze occurs in the poem.

dizzy.why: Hector reels and drops when Ajax's boulder strikes him, and darkness covers the eyes of many falling warriors, but faintness is only a passing note.

fatigued.why: Ajax's arm grows weary and sweat pours as he alone defends the ships, and Hector and Achilles race three laps around the walls of Troy.

pain.why: Spears pierce bladders, teeth, and brains across hundreds of deaths; Diomedes, Agamemnon, Odysseus, and even Aphrodite and Ares cry out from their wounds.

disgusted.why: Dogs and birds feed on corpses, Thetis must keep flies from Patroclus' wounds, and Ajax slips face-first into ox dung during the funeral games.

itchy.why: Nothing itches anyone in the poem.

over-stimulated.why: The Myrmidons cannot look straight at Achilles' new armor, and his shout from the ditch, amplified by Athena, throws the Trojans into chaos.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Hephaestus's fire boils the river Scamander and scorches the plain, and the sun's heat hangs over the fighting, but temperature rarely troubles the characters.

afraid.why: Fear rules the battlefield: Paris shrinks from Menelaus, the Trojans flee Achilles' war cry, and Hector himself runs three laps around the walls before facing him.

anxious.why: Andromache dreads widowhood, Hector foresees the day Troy falls, Priam fears for his remaining sons, and Achilles lives knowing his own death follows Hector's.

panic.why: Rout follows rout: the Greeks break for the ships under Hector, the Trojans tumble into the Scamander before Achilles, and Hector flees from him in terror.

sensory-pleasures.why: Heroes feast on roasted meat and wine, Zeus and Hera lie together on Ida wrapped in a golden cloud, and Achilles sleeps beside Briseis.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Achilles sings of heroes' deeds to his lyre when the embassy arrives, and Hephaestus's shield, described at length, is a marvel of craft.

fun-excitement.why: The funeral games for Patroclus, with the chariot race, boxing, wrestling, and footrace, give the heroes a day of contest and prizes.

orgasm.why: Zeus and Hera make love on Mount Ida and Paris takes Helen to bed after his duel, but the poem passes over the act itself.

love-romantic.why: Hector and Andromache's farewell at the gate, Paris's desire for Helen that began the war, and Achilles' avowed love for Briseis run through the poem.

love-family.why: Thetis grieves for her doomed son, Priam kisses the hands that killed Hector to recover his body, and Hector lifts Astyanax to pray for him.

grief.why: Achilles pours dust over his head for Patroclus, Zeus weeps tears of blood for Sarpedon, and the poem ends with the laments of Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen.

missing-someone.why: Patroclus' ghost begs Achilles for burial so they can be together again, and Helen looks from the wall for her brothers, not knowing they are dead.

aroused-sexually.why: Paris, fresh from his duel, tells Helen desire has never gripped him so, and Zeus, under Hera's borrowed girdle, wants her more than any past lover.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Achilles' bond with Patroclus drives the second half, Diomedes and Odysseus raid together, and Glaucus and Diomedes trade armor as guest-friends mid-battle.

empathy.why: Patroclus weeps for the wounded Greeks, and Achilles, seeing Priam, thinks of his own father Peleus and weeps with him.

compassion.why: Achilles pities Priam and returns Hector's body, Zeus pities Achilles' immortal horses weeping for Patroclus, and Patroclus pleads for the dying Greeks.

grateful.why: Chryses thanks Apollo for the plague, and Priam blesses Achilles for returning Hector's body, but gratitude seldom shapes the heroes' dealings.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nestor delights in counseling the kings, and Patroclus tends the wounded Eurypylus, but the poem seldom dwells on satisfaction taken from helping.

trustful-distrustful.why: Achilles will not trust Agamemnon's gifts after the theft of Briseis, Pandarus breaks the sworn truce, and Athena, disguised as Deiphobus, dupes Hector into standing his ground.

depressed.why: Achilles, grieving Patroclus, wishes only to die, and Helen, despised in Troy, says she has no one but Hector and Priam to turn to.

angry.why: Wrath is the poem's first word: Achilles' fury at Agamemnon's insult withdraws him from the war, and his fury at Hector returns him to it.

envious.why: Achilles complains that Agamemnon takes the richest prize while he bears the brunt of fighting, and the kings measure their honor against each other's shares.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: The war springs from Paris taking Helen from Menelaus, Achilles rages that Agamemnon took the woman he loved, and Hera resents Zeus's affairs.

jealous-friendship.why: No character fears losing a friend's favor to a rival; the bonds between Achilles and Patroclus and among the kings face no such competition.

hatred.why: Achilles hates Agamemnon, who stripped him of his prize, then Hector, who killed Patroclus, wishing he could eat his flesh raw; Hera's hatred of Troy never relents.

contempt.why: Achilles calls Agamemnon dog-faced and deer-hearted, Hector scorns Paris as a pretty-boy womanizer, and Odysseus beats the scurrilous Thersites into silence.

resentment.why: Achilles' sense that Agamemnon has robbed him of his rightful prize sends him to Thetis and Zeus for redress, and Thersites voices the ranks' grievance over unfair shares.

proud.why: The code of honor and glory rules every warrior: Hector will not shelter behind the walls lest Polydamas reproach him, and Achilles chooses glory over long life.

amused.why: The gods break into unquenchable laughter when Hephaestus bustles about as cupbearer, and the Greeks laugh at Ajax spitting out ox dung in the footrace.

sense-of-belonging.why: Achilles cuts himself off from the Achaean host and his Myrmidons chafe in idleness until he rejoins the army and is formally reconciled with Agamemnon.

lonely.why: Achilles weeps alone on the shore after losing Briseis, and Helen, friendless in Troy, says only Hector and Priam were ever kind to her.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The gods condemn Achilles' abuse of Hector's corpse, the Achaeans judge Agamemnon in the wrong, and the Trojans blame Paris for the war.

admiration.why: Priam and Helen admire the Greek champions from the wall, Priam marvels at Achilles' size and beauty, and warriors on both sides praise Hector's prowess.

embarrassed.why: Paris, rebuked by Hector for shrinking from Menelaus, admits the reproach is deserved, but embarrassment is a minor note beside shame.

shame.why: Hector stays outside the walls because he cannot bear the Trojans' reproach, Helen calls herself a shameless bitch, and Agamemnon admits his folly before the assembly.

guilt.why: Achilles blames himself for letting Patroclus die, Helen reproaches herself for the war, and Agamemnon admits that delusion led him to wrong Achilles.

sad.why: Achilles weeps by the sea over the loss of Briseis, Andromache mourns the family Achilles already killed, and sorrow hangs over Troy's doomed defenders.

happy.why: Contentment is brief: Hector smiles at his son, and the Achaeans cheer Achilles' return, but no character's life is going well overall.

joyful-euphoric.why: Hector exults stripping Patroclus' armor, the Trojans rejoice at breaching the wall, and Achilles' eyes blaze with delight at his new armor from Hephaestus.

effort.why: Ajax holds the ships though his shoulder aches under the shield, Achilles chases Hector three laps, and the war grinds on into its tenth year.

focused-in-flow.why: The aristeiai of Diomedes, Agamemnon, Patroclus, and Achilles are sustained rampages in which one warrior sweeps the field in total absorption.

bored.why: Achilles sits idle by his ships, longing for the war cry and battle, while his Myrmidons chafe at inaction.

distracted.why: Hera seduces Zeus so his attention leaves the battlefield, letting Poseidon rally the Greeks, and Patroclus, caught up in slaughter, forgets Achilles' orders.

impatient.why: After Patroclus' death Achilles cannot wait for the army to eat and urges immediate battle, and Agamemnon chafes through the long siege.

curious.why: Priam asks Helen to name the Achaean chiefs from the wall, and both armies send spies, Dolon and then Odysseus and Diomedes, to learn the other's plans.

surprised.why: Achilles starts in amazement when Priam appears unannounced in his tent, and Hector is stunned to find Deiphobus gone and himself alone before Achilles.

awe.why: Warriors stand in dread wonder at the gods' manifestations, at Zeus's thunder and Achilles' blazing armor, and the heroes marvel at Hephaestus's shield.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Hector dismisses Polydamas's bird omen as worthless, and Hecuba doubts that Achilles will spare Priam if he goes to the Greek camp.

feeling-of-knowing.why: No character strains to recall something half-remembered; what the heroes know is told to them by gods, heralds, and Nestor.

confused.why: Agamemnon's test of the army backfires into a rush for the ships, and Hector, calling for Deiphobus's spear, finds no one there and grasps Athena's trick.

frustrated.why: Menelaus finds his sword shattered and Paris whisked away by Aphrodite, Achilles cannot catch Hector until Athena intervenes, and the embassy fails to move him.

uncertain-certain.why: Achilles hesitates whether to draw on Agamemnon until Athena stops him, Hector debates with himself before the gate, and Zeus weighs Hector's fate on golden scales.

understanding.why: Achilles, facing Priam, arrives at his understanding of the two urns of Zeus, that grief is the common lot of mortals.

inspired.why: Nestor hits on the plan that Patroclus wear Achilles' armor, and Hera devises the seduction of Zeus to free Poseidon's hand.

satisfied.why: Priam achieves his purpose and Hector is buried, but Achilles, even after killing Hector, finds no satisfaction and keeps dragging the corpse.

foreboding.why: Thetis knows Achilles dies soon after Hector, Hector foresees Troy burning and Andromache enslaved, and Zeus names each hero's doom before it comes.

nostalgia.why: Nestor recalls at length the warriors of his youth, and Achilles and Priam both look back to Peleus and happier days.

anticipation-suspense.why: The Greeks wait through book after book for Achilles to return, and Priam's night journey through the enemy camp holds everyone in dread until he reaches Achilles.

hope.why: Hector hopes to burn the ships and end the war, the Greeks hope Achilles will relent, and Priam goes to the Greek camp hoping to buy back his son.

schadenfreude.why: Achilles gloats over the dying Hector and the Greeks stab the corpse in turn, the army laughs at Thersites' beating, and Athena mocks the wounded Aphrodite.

elevation.why: The meeting of Priam and Achilles, two enemies weeping together over their dead, is the poem's moment of moral uplift.

infatuation.why: Paris is besotted with Helen, and Zeus, under Aphrodite's girdle, is briefly infatuated with Hera.

rage.why: Achilles' rampage after Patroclus' death, slaughtering Trojans, choking the river with corpses, and dragging Hector's body, is rage beyond anger.
